### Safety parts we’ll touch | Feature | What we’ll do | |---------|---------------| | **Logins with email only** | Add a simple “**verify**” step so the user really owns the address, and set a short‑term magic‑link expiry. | | **Prevent fake sign‑ups** | Add a cheap captcha (e.g., hCaptcha or reCAPTCHA) or a “honeypot” field so bots can’t register. | | **Keep your database rules tight** | Make sure only the person who just signed up can see their own row; this stops someone from creating many accounts that look personal. | | **Monitor** | Turn on an email notification for every new account so you can spot suspicious batches quickly. | --- ## Quick checklist (no code yet) 1. **Ask you a couple of quick questions** – if anything below is unknown, let me know and I’ll guide you. 2. **Give you the exact changes** (copy‑paste snippets) and where to place them. 3. **Explain how to test** it locally (or in the Supabase Studio UI) so you can see it works before we push anything live. 4. **Save a checkpoint** first so you can rollback if needed. --- ### 1️⃣ Questions 1. *Do you already use Supabase Auth’s magic‑link (email‑only) flow?* 2. *Is your sign‑up page just a plain form that calls `supabase.auth.signUp()`?* 3. *Do you currently have email verification turned on in your Supabase Project settings?* 4. *Do you mind adding a free captcha box (hCaptcha has a simple one‑line package) or a simple “honeypot” trick?* Feel free to skip any you’re sure about; we’ll just add that part. --- ### 2️⃣ What we’ll add #### a) Force email verification In your Supabase Project, go to **Authentication → Settings → Email** and enable “Require email confirmation”. That makes the user click a link that we send; bots can’t do that. #### b) Short‑lived magic links Supabase automatically sends a link that expires in 60 minutes (you can change it). If you want a stricter expiry: ```ts // Replace with your own email handler if you have one await supabase.auth.signUp({ email: userEmail, options: { emailRedirectTo: "https://your-site.com/redirect" }, }); ``` The `emailRedirectTo` URL will be opened by the magic link; you can add a “verify” button there. #### c) Add a honeypot field Add a hidden field to your form (e.g., `id="website"`). Code that tries to submit a value will be filtered out: ```html ``` In your form‑handler, ignore or delete that field before calling `supabase.auth.signUp()`. #### d) (Optional) Tiny captcha Use hCaptcha’s free “inline” widget: ```html
``` Add the matching verification server‑side: ```ts const token = formData.get('h-captcha'); await fetch("https://hcaptcha.com/siteverify", { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams({ secret: "YOUR_HCAPTCHA_SECRET", response: token, }), }); ``` If the captcha fails, reject the sign‑up. --- ### 3️⃣ Testing locally 1. **Create a test email** (e.g., `test@example.com`). 2. **Submit the form** → you should get a confirmation email with a link. 3. **Click the link** → you’re logged in. 4. Submit the form again with the hidden `website` field set → you should see that the row wasn’t created. 5. Try guessing the captcha (leave it empty) → sign‑up fails. If everything works, you’re good to go. --- ### 4️⃣ Save a checkpoint Before you touch your project: 1. **Commit** (or zip) your current files. 2. In Supabase Studio, go to **Table Editor → Email Verification Table** and export a backup of `auth.users`. 3. Keep the backup in a safe place; you’ll need it only if something goes wrong. --- ## TL;DR – one‑liner cheat sheet 1. Enable **“Require email confirmation”** in Supabase Auth settings. 2. Add a hidden **honeypot field** (`id="website"`) to the sign‑up form. 3. (Optional) Add an **hCaptcha** widget and verify the token server‑side. 4. Test with a fresh email → confirm email click → verify that the honeypot blocks bots. 5. Commit a checkpoint before any changes. Let me know which questions above are already answered or if you’d like a step‑by‑step guide for any of the additions. We’ll keep it simple and safe.
